shortDescription: Older healing systems, folk knowledge, herbal practices, or traditional medicine are framed as wiser, safer, and more human than modern medicine — and as something deliberately forgotten or displaced.
likelyDistortion: Older healing systems are more truthful and humane; modern medicine displaced them for profit, control, or prestige; forgetting was deliberate not accidental.
publicFear: That institutional medicine has alienated us from real human care and effective traditional knowledge.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Respect for traditional knowledge does not require rejecting modern medicine. Many traditional practices are actively studied and integrated. The 'displacement' narrative usually conflates progress with suppression.
whatItDoesNotMean: Appreciating traditional or herbal medicine is not anti-science. The distortion comes from framing displacement as deliberate and modern medicine as inherently alienating.
rapidResponseAdvice: Acknowledge value in traditional knowledge without accepting the conspiracy of deliberate forgetting. Point to active research in ethnobotany, integrative medicine, and pharmacological study of traditional compounds. Distinguish between 'lost' and 'evidence-tested'.
humourOptions: My grandmother also knew that willow bark tea worked. We call it aspirin now.
Yes, traditional medicine was pushed aside. By better outcomes.
The real tragedy is not that we forgot traditional healing. It's that we forget how recently traditional healing forgot to wash its hands.
exampleNarrative: We already knew how to heal. Then modern medicine taught us to forget.
notes: This frame overlaps with natural body absolutism and often appears in anti-pharma narratives. It gains traction in chronic illness and fertility spaces where modern medicine has failed to deliver easy answers.

shortDescription: Research is framed as concealed knowledge withheld from ordinary people.
likelyDistortion: Scientists or institutions are hiding harms, costs, or motives.
publicFear: Loss of agency; betrayal by experts
whatToClarifyUpfront: State scope, evidence standard, and what is known vs unknown.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not prove concealment or coordinated intent.
rapidResponseAdvice: Lead with plain facts and process transparency; avoid defensive jargon.
humourOptions: Nuance has poor survival odds online. Help it out.
exampleNarrative: They knew this all along and never told the public.
notes: Good default frame for anything involving trust or expertise.

shortDescription: Scientific work is recast as profit-driven collusion between labs, funders, firms, or governments.
likelyDistortion: The study exists to serve commercial or elite interests rather than evidence.
publicFear: Being exploited for money or power
whatToClarifyUpfront: Name funding, trial phase, limits, and oversight mechanisms.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not imply commercial deployment or hidden financial coordination.
rapidResponseAdvice: Clarify who funded what, and what the research stage actually is.
humourOptions: Sadly, a funding disclosure is less viral than a conspiracy.
exampleNarrative: This is just another elite pipeline for profit.
notes: Especially relevant when the abstract mentions therapy, trial, platform, rollout.

shortDescription: Research is portrayed as unnatural intervention in life, bodies, ecosystems, or human identity.
likelyDistortion: Scientists are redesigning nature or humanity without consent.
publicFear: Bodily integrity; moral contamination; loss of what is natural
whatToClarifyUpfront: Stress research stage, safeguards, and limited scope.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not imply public deployment, redesign of humanity, or removal of consent.
rapidResponseAdvice: Separate mechanism discovery from real-world application.
humourOptions: Apparently every pipette is a plot to redesign civilisation.
exampleNarrative: They are playing God with nature and calling it science.
notes: Useful for biotech, embryo work, gene editing, ecological manipulation.

shortDescription: The research is reframed as a threat to children, families, or future generations.
likelyDistortion: The work is twisted into a story about harm to children or families.
publicFear: Protection of children and kin
whatToClarifyUpfront: Be explicit about who the study is and is not about.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not imply direct risk to children, fertility, or parenting.
rapidResponseAdvice: Correct the target population and do not repeat the scare frame.
humourOptions: Nothing says sober research debate like 'what about the children?' five minutes in.
exampleNarrative: This will harm children and they know it.
notes: Often appears even when children are not actually in scope.

shortDescription: A finding is reframed as proof that society, morality, or institutions are collapsing.
likelyDistortion: A bounded finding becomes evidence of broad societal breakdown.
publicFear: Status loss; moral panic; identity threat
whatToClarifyUpfront: Restate the narrow research question and the limits of generalisation.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not prove large-scale decline or cultural takeover.
rapidResponseAdvice: Shrink the frame back to the actual population and method.
humourOptions: One dataset is not, in fact, the fall of civilisation.
exampleNarrative: This proves our society is collapsing.
notes: Useful when abstracts touch values, identity, or institutions.

shortDescription: Research is framed as frivolous, ideological, or detached from ordinary people's needs.
likelyDistortion: The research is a luxury hobby funded by the public against their interests.
publicFear: Resentment of elite institutions
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain practical value, limits, and why exploratory work matters.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not imply immediate policy cost or elite contempt.
rapidResponseAdvice: Translate why the question matters in plain language.
humourOptions: The taxpayer-funded apocalypse apparently now includes basic research.
exampleNarrative: They waste public money on ideological nonsense.
notes: Good for publicly funded academic work.

shortDescription: Scientific consensus is reframed as silencing dissent or punishing common sense.
likelyDistortion: Evidence-based messaging is recast as elite suppression.
publicFear: Loss of voice; social punishment
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain what is evidence, what is uncertainty, and what is moderation vs debate.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not prove censorship or suppression of legitimate inquiry.
rapidResponseAdvice: Avoid sounding punitive; emphasise clarification not shaming.
humourOptions: The internet does love calling correction 'censorship'.
exampleNarrative: They want to silence anyone asking questions.
notes: Especially relevant for contentious health or platform topics.

shortDescription: Research is recast as a pretext for regulation, behavioural control, or social engineering.
likelyDistortion: The finding is used as evidence of top-down control over everyday life.
publicFear: Loss of autonomy; coercion
whatToClarifyUpfront: Separate evidence generation from policy choices and implementation.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not itself justify mandates, surveillance, or coercive policy.
rapidResponseAdvice: Say clearly what the study informs and what it does not authorise.
humourOptions: A correlation paper is not a coup, despite appearances online.
exampleNarrative: This is about controlling the public, not science.
notes: Good for topics adjacent to policy or governance.

shortDescription: A normal research community is reframed as a coordinated clique protecting its own power, grants, and worldview.
likelyDistortion: Scientists are acting together as a self-serving caste rather than as a contested evidence community.
publicFear: Exclusion by insiders; rigged expertise; loss of public voice
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain how disagreement, replication, review, and oversight actually work; name uncertainty and institutional limits.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not show central coordination, uniform intent, or a single scientific line imposed from above.
rapidResponseAdvice: Demystify process. Show where scientists disagree, and where guardrails exist. Keep the tone calm, not priestly.
humourOptions: It is a lab meeting, not a moon cult.
A research network is not automatically a secret society, however disappointing that may be for the plot.
exampleNarrative: “They all cite each other, fund each other, and call it science.”
notes: Useful across topics. Especially relevant for NATO / hybrid-warfare style work on institutional mistrust.

frameName: Prevention is withheld because treatment pays
shortDescription: Research, guidance, or clinical priorities are framed as intentionally favouring profitable treatment over prevention.
likelyDistortion: Institutions suppress low-cost prevention because recurring treatment is more lucrative.
publicFear: People are being kept chronically ill on purpose.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Differentiate prevention, risk reduction, treatment, and evidence thresholds. Explain why proving prevention claims is hard and why that does not imply bad faith.
whatItDoesNotMean: A study on treatment does not prove prevention is ignored, and commercial incentives do not erase evidentiary standards.
rapidResponseAdvice: Acknowledge the intuition behind the suspicion, then explain pathways, incentives, and evidence in plain language.
humourOptions: The spreadsheet of incentives is real. The giant master plan usually is not.
The spreadsheet is not secretly dating the tumour.
exampleNarrative: “If they wanted you healthy, this would be front-page news.”
notes: Very relevant to food, sunscreen, metabolic health, and supplement rhetoric.

shortDescription: Low-dose exposure, residues, additives, or particles are framed as proof of widespread hidden poisoning.
likelyDistortion: Any detectable substance becomes evidence of deliberate harm or systemic negligence.
publicFear: The body is under constant assault from invisible industrial chemicals.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Separate detection from danger. Explain dose, route, context, uncertainty, and what regulators actually measure.
whatItDoesNotMean: Detection alone does not equal clinically meaningful risk, and “chemical” is not a synonym for harm.
rapidResponseAdvice: Use one crisp comparison and one visual. Avoid over-reassurance; explain thresholds and uncertainty.
humourOptions: Modern instruments can detect almost everything. They cannot automatically tell you what deserves panic.
Yes, a particle is small. No, it is not automatically plotting against you.
exampleNarrative: “If they can measure it, it must already be poisoning you.”
notes: Use whenever nanoparticles, sunscreen, additives, residues, or biomonitoring appear.

shortDescription: Digital health tools are framed as a pretext for monitoring, behavioural control, or loss of bodily autonomy.
likelyDistortion: Medical infrastructure is presented as creeping social control disguised as convenience or safety.
publicFear: Health data will be used against ordinary people by states, insurers, or platforms.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Clarify what data is collected, who can access it, what safeguards exist, and where the limits are.
whatItDoesNotMean: Digitisation is not identical to coercion, and interoperability does not automatically imply surveillance.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name governance mechanisms, retention limits, and opt-out boundaries. Be concrete, not soothing.
humourOptions: A medical record is not a spy thriller, though poor governance can certainly audition for one.
A better database is not, by itself, the panopticon in a white coat.
exampleNarrative: “Today a health app, tomorrow a citizen score.”
notes: Relevant to WHO, digital IDs, eHealth, and institutional trust.

shortDescription: Low-cost compounds, supplements, or repurposed interventions are framed as deliberately buried because they threaten profitable medicine.
triggerWords: they do not want you to know
likelyDistortion: A simple cure exists but is being hidden by regulators, industry, or “medical elites”.
publicFear: Life-saving solutions are being withheld for profit.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain what counts as evidence, approval, dosing, replication, and clinical relevance.
whatItDoesNotMean: A promising mechanism, lab result, or anecdote is not the same thing as a proven cure.
rapidResponseAdvice: Respond quickly and plainly. Name the gap between interesting early evidence and treatment-grade proof.
humourOptions: A molecule can be promising without already deserving its own conspiracy documentary.
exampleNarrative: “This doctor will be deleted in 24 hours for telling the truth.”
notes: Useful for deepfake doctors and miracle-cure sales.

shortDescription: Biological “naturalness” is framed as morally and medically superior to vaccination, additives, or any engineered intervention.
likelyDistortion: Intervention is treated as corruption of a perfect natural system.
publicFear: The body is self-sufficient and modern medicine weakens it.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Acknowledge that bodies are adaptive without romanticising vulnerability. Explain risk trade-offs and context.
whatItDoesNotMean: Natural exposure is not automatically safer, and “natural” is not a scientific verdict.
rapidResponseAdvice: Keep this calm and non-patronising. Moral language around purity escalates quickly.
humourOptions: Nature does many admirable things. It also, on occasion, invents measles.
exampleNarrative: “Your immune system is perfect until science interferes.”
notes: High relevance for routine vaccination and wellness content. This frame often spills into pregnancy politics, where the 'natural course' is moralised and medical intervention is cast as contamination, weakness, or civilisational decay.

shortDescription: International coordination in health is framed as a cover for coercion, sovereignty loss, or mass behavioural control.
likelyDistortion: Health governance is reinterpreted as supranational domination.
publicFear: National self-rule is being replaced by unelected medical control.
whatToClarifyUpfront: State clearly what is voluntary, what is binding, and who holds authority. Separate coordination from coercion.
whatItDoesNotMean: International agreements do not automatically erase national decision-making.
rapidResponseAdvice: Use institutional diagrams, not abstractions. People need to see who can and cannot do what.
humourOptions: An acronym is not yet a coup, however theatrical the caption.
exampleNarrative: “Public health is the excuse; global control is the project.”
notes: Useful for WHO / pandemic treaty disinformation.

shortDescription: Mental-health expertise is framed as a machinery of numbing, labelling, and dependency rather than care.
likelyDistortion: Professional care is cast as social control while quick hacks or self-diagnosis are sold as liberation.
publicFear: People are being chemically managed instead of understood.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Differentiate symptom relief, long-term care, diagnosis, and evidence. Avoid overstating what one study can do.
whatItDoesNotMean: A critique of over-medicalisation is not proof that expertise is fake, and a viral trick is not treatment.
rapidResponseAdvice: Stay humane. Mental-health discussions punish cold language instantly.
humourOptions: The existence of nuance is inconvenient for anyone selling a 60-second cure.
exampleNarrative: “Psychiatrists want subscribers; here is the one breathing trick they fear.”
notes: Relevant to Gen Z self-diagnosis and pseudo-therapeutic content.

shortDescription: Research on society is framed as activist doctrine disguised as evidence.
likelyDistortion: The work is recast as political preaching rather than analysis.
publicFear: fear of indoctrination, elite contempt, social engineering
whatToClarifyUpfront: State clearly what was measured, how, and where interpretation begins.
whatItDoesNotMean: It does not prove a moral ranking of citizens or justify coercive redesign of society.
rapidResponseAdvice: Lead with method, sample limits, and plain-language definitions before values-based debates hijack the story.
humourOptions: Careful sociology can still be accused of having opinions in a lab coat.
exampleNarrative: “They call it research, but it is just ideology with charts.”
notes: Useful for sociology, education, migration, trust, and inequality topics.

shortDescription: Economic hardship is framed as intentional harm imposed by elites, experts, or global agendas.
likelyDistortion: Findings are twisted into a story that experts want ordinary people poorer, weaker, or more dependent.
publicFear: fear of engineered decline, loss of livelihood, class resentment
whatToClarifyUpfront: Separate descriptive analysis from policy preference and explain trade-offs clearly.
whatItDoesNotMean: It does not prove a plot to impoverish households or abolish prosperity.
rapidResponseAdvice: Acknowledge real costs openly; vagueness about winners and losers invites conspiracy language.
humourOptions: An elasticity estimate can become a class-war poster very quickly.
exampleNarrative: “This is not economics, it is a blueprint for making you poorer.”
notes: Useful for economics, labour, taxation, transition, and energy policy.

shortDescription: Research touching schools, child development, literacy, or public communication is framed as ideological conditioning.
likelyDistortion: Normal educational or preventive work is recast as state-sponsored brainwashing.
publicFear: fear of parental displacement, moral capture, loss of family authority
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain the educational goal, age group, and practical boundaries in very plain language.
whatItDoesNotMean: It does not replace parents, erase disagreement, or programme children into one worldview.
rapidResponseAdvice: Show the concrete classroom purpose and who decides what is taught.
humourOptions: The phrase “resilience training” can sound heroic to you and suspicious to somebody else’s uncle.
exampleNarrative: “They are not teaching children; they are programming them.”
notes: Useful for education, literacy, misinformation, and child-development topics.

shortDescription: Evidence-based policy advice is reframed as rule by unelected specialists who bypass democratic legitimacy.
likelyDistortion: Research is portrayed as an instrument for replacing politics with technocratic command.
publicFear: fear of lost sovereignty, democratic bypass, unaccountable control
whatToClarifyUpfront: Clarify the difference between evidence, advice, and political decision-making.
whatItDoesNotMean: It does not grant scientists the authority to rule, punish, or legislate.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name who decides, who advises, and what remains contested.
humourOptions: A policy brief is not a coup, though the internet may file it under one.
exampleNarrative: “Experts now think they should govern instead of elected people.”
notes: Useful for policy, regulation, WHO, education, economics, and climate topics.

shortDescription: Historical research is framed as an attempt to shame, weaken, or delegitimise the nation through selective memory.
likelyDistortion: Findings are twisted into claims that historians are erasing pride and manufacturing national self-hatred.
publicFear: fear of humiliation, identity loss, betrayal of ancestors
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain the scope of the archive, period, and research question before moral conclusions rush in.
whatItDoesNotMean: It does not declare the nation uniquely evil or demand collective guilt from living citizens.
rapidResponseAdvice: Distinguish historical explanation from present-day moral accusation.
humourOptions: An archive note can be rebranded as treason before lunch.
exampleNarrative: “They are rewriting history so you will be ashamed of your own country.”
notes: Useful for history, war memory, empire, education, and identity debates.

shortDescription: Population research is recast as proof of a coordinated plan to replace, dilute, or outnumber the “real” population.
likelyDistortion: Descriptive research becomes a civilisational emergency narrative about invasion and disappearance.
publicFear: fear of extinction, loss of continuity, ethnic panic
whatToClarifyUpfront: State what the numbers do and do not show; define time horizons and uncertainty.
whatItDoesNotMean: It does not prove intentional replacement, imminent collapse, or zero-sum demographic war.
rapidResponseAdvice: Avoid compressed phrasing that sounds like a countdown to national extinction.
humourOptions: A population chart can acquire battle music in under five minutes.
exampleNarrative: “The data prove they are replacing us.”
notes: Useful for migration, fertility, demography, urban studies, and religion topics.

shortDescription: Research is framed as the product of foreign influence, globalist ideology, or external interference in national life.
likelyDistortion: Findings are twisted into evidence that international or foreign actors are directing national policy against the interests of citizens.
publicFear: Loss of national sovereignty; manipulation by unseen external powers
whatToClarifyUpfront: State clearly who funded the research, where it was conducted, and what decisions it can and cannot influence.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not mean the research serves a foreign political agenda or overrides national democratic decisions.
rapidResponseAdvice: Be concrete about institutional affiliations and funding. Abstract denials of 'foreign influence' tend to amplify the frame.
humourOptions: The data did not arrive by diplomatic pouch.
A co-authored paper is not a geopolitical operation, despite what the caption says.
exampleNarrative: This research was funded by globalist institutions to force their agenda on us.
notes: Critical for NATO/cognitive-security context and hybrid-threat environments. Especially relevant in Central and Eastern Europe.

frameName: Science as weapon of cultural war
shortDescription: Research on values, identity, behaviour, or society is framed as one side of a culture war rather than as inquiry.
likelyDistortion: Findings are recast as evidence that researchers are political activists using data to delegitimise traditional values or reshape society.
publicFear: Moral displacement; loss of cultural identity; imposition of minority values on majority
whatToClarifyUpfront: Separate what was measured from what is being recommended. State the method and sample clearly before interpretations are made.
whatItDoesNotMean: It does not declare one set of values superior, endorse political positions, or prescribe how society should be organised.
rapidResponseAdvice: Lead with methodology before values language. Avoid terms that are already coded in the culture-war lexicon without defining them precisely.
humourOptions: A survey is not a manifesto, even when it produces inconvenient results.
Measuring something is not the same as endorsing it. This remains true regardless of what the something is.
exampleNarrative: This is not research — it is woke ideology dressed up in statistics.
notes: Increasingly relevant across social science, education, and policy research in polarised environments.

shortDescription: Research using population data, health records, or behavioural datasets is framed as covert surveillance or exploitation of people without their knowledge.
likelyDistortion: Normal data governance and research ethics procedures are dismissed; the research is recast as violation of privacy and bodily autonomy.
publicFear: Being studied, profiled, or exploited without knowledge or recourse
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain what data was used, how it was anonymised, what ethics approval was granted, and what participants were told.
whatItDoesNotMean: Using anonymised or consented population data is not covert surveillance, and published findings are not a commercial data product.
rapidResponseAdvice: Be specific about consent, anonymisation, and governance. Vague reassurances increase distrust.
humourOptions: The ethics committee exists and it did, in fact, read the protocol.
Anonymised aggregate data is not your file. It is, at best, a very blurry crowd scene.
exampleNarrative: They used our health data without asking and now they are profiting from it.
notes: Growing relevance for digital health, AI, epidemiology, and any research using admin or platform data.

shortDescription: AI-generated content mimics medical expertise, producing confident-sounding diagnoses, treatment advice, or expert endorsements that carry no clinical accountability.
likelyDistortion: AI-produced medical content is treated as equivalent to clinical expertise. Synthetic confidence replaces accountability, qualifications, and clinical context.
publicFear: Being given medical advice by a machine pretending to be a doctor — and not knowing the difference
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain what role AI played in the research or communication, who holds clinical responsibility, and what human oversight applies.
whatItDoesNotMean: AI assistance in research or diagnostics does not mean a machine is replacing your doctor, and AI-generated text is not a peer-reviewed clinical recommendation.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name the boundary between AI assistance and clinical responsibility. The public needs to know who is accountable, not just who is confident.
humourOptions: The algorithm has excellent bedside manner. No actual bedside, though.
It passed the confidence exam. Still working on the medical one.
exampleNarrative: This AI doctor diagnosed me in seconds — no waiting room, no judgement. Why do we still need real doctors?
notes: Covers deepfake experts, synthetic health influencers, and AI systems presenting with false clinical authority.

shortDescription: Early-stage, preliminary, or non-peer-reviewed findings are presented as settled fact, stripping away the uncertainty, replication needs, and caveats that define how science actually works.
likelyDistortion: A single preliminary finding is elevated to proof. Caveats about sample size, study design, and replication are stripped away, creating false certainty.
publicFear: Being told something is true when it might not be — and making decisions based on it
whatToClarifyUpfront: State clearly what stage this evidence is at — preprint, pilot, phase 1, single study — and what would be needed to confirm the finding.
whatItDoesNotMean: A preliminary or early finding is not proof. It is a signal that warrants further investigation, not a basis for public health decisions or personal choices.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name the evidence stage. One sentence about what was found, one about what it does not yet prove, and one about what happens next.
humourOptions: One study is a conversation starter, not a mic drop.
Preliminary means 'interesting, keep going' — not 'stop the presses.'
exampleNarrative: Scientists have confirmed that this compound cures the disease — the study is right here.
notes: Cross-domain pattern. Applies to health, environment, nutrition, psychology, and technology. One of the most common distortion patterns in science communication.

shortDescription: Commercial wellness products or alternative health claims borrow the language and aesthetics of science without meeting its standards, creating a veneer of evidence for unproven interventions.
likelyDistortion: Commercial products use scientific-sounding language to create false authority. The claim sounds evidence-based but the evidence is absent, cherry-picked, or inapplicable.
publicFear: Missing out on something that works because 'mainstream science' is too slow or too compromised to recognise it
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain what the actual evidence base is for the claim. Distinguish between scientific language and scientific evidence. Name the standard the claim would need to meet.
whatItDoesNotMean: Using scientific-sounding words does not make something scientific. 'Clinically proven' on a product label does not mean the same thing as clinical proof in a peer-reviewed study.
rapidResponseAdvice: Don't attack the product. Explain the gap between the language being used and the evidence that would justify it. Let the audience see the mismatch.
humourOptions: If 'science-backed' meant what Instagram thinks it means, we'd have cured everything by now.
The supplement has a PhD in graphic design.
exampleNarrative: This natural supplement is clinically proven to boost immunity — doctors don't want you to know because they can't profit from it.
notes: Often commercially motivated rather than conspiratorial. Important to treat the audience with respect — many people genuinely want better health options.

shortDescription: Exaggerated or distorted claims about threats to fertility, hormones, or reproductive health — often targeting younger audiences with fear-based content about products, exposures, or institutions damaging their bodies.
likelyDistortion: Narrow findings about hormonal mechanisms or reproductive markers are inflated into existential threats to fertility, often linking them to products, policies, or institutions as deliberate attacks.
publicFear: That something is silently damaging your ability to have children — and no one is telling you
whatToClarifyUpfront: Specify what was actually measured, in what population, with what effect size. Distinguish between a hormonal signal and a fertility outcome. Name what is known and what is not.
whatItDoesNotMean: A hormonal measurement in a laboratory study does not mean your fertility is under attack. A change in a biomarker is not the same as a change in reproductive outcomes.
rapidResponseAdvice: Restore scale. Name what was measured and what was not. Acknowledge that reproductive health matters — then explain why this finding does not mean what the panic version says it means.
humourOptions: Your hormones have survived worse than this study's abstract.
Sperm counts: the one statistic where everyone suddenly cares about methodology.
exampleNarrative: They are putting chemicals in everything that are destroying our fertility and nobody is doing anything about it.
notes: Particularly prevalent on social media targeting younger audiences. Often mixes legitimate concern with commercial supplement marketing. This frame often overlaps with contraception narratives (F40), where side effects, hormonal changes, and fertility anxiety are pulled into a wider moral story about femininity, decline, and control. Also overlaps with F42 (disease as unresolved inner conflict), where hormonal and fertility issues are interpreted through a lens of moral failure, inner conflict, or spiritual imbalance rather than medical causation.

shortDescription: The volume and complexity of available information is reframed as deliberate institutional strategy — 'they flood you with information so you stop knowing what is true' — turning confusion into evidence of conspiracy.
likelyDistortion: The natural complexity of science and public communication is recast as intentional manipulation. Confusion becomes proof of a cover-up rather than a feature of difficult topics.
publicFear: That the sheer volume of contradictory information is a deliberate strategy to prevent you from knowing the truth
whatToClarifyUpfront: Acknowledge that science communication is genuinely complex and that confusion is understandable. Explain why contradictory findings exist and how evidence accumulates over time.
whatItDoesNotMean: Complexity is not conspiracy. Contradictory findings are a normal part of science, not evidence that someone is hiding the truth. Difficulty understanding something does not mean it was designed to confuse you.
rapidResponseAdvice: Validate the frustration. Explain that uncertainty is real but not engineered. Help the audience see how evidence works without sounding condescending.
humourOptions: Science is confusing because reality is confusing. That is not a plot twist.
If they wanted to hide the truth, publishing thousands of open-access papers is a strange strategy.
exampleNarrative: They keep changing the guidelines on purpose so no one knows what to believe anymore. It's deliberate.
notes: A meta-narrative that can attach to any topic. Particularly dangerous because it makes all correction look like further manipulation.

shortDescription: Disease outbreaks or health risks are attributed to migrants, refugees, or foreign populations — using epidemiological language to justify exclusion and frame outsiders as biological threats.
likelyDistortion: Health data about disease prevalence is selectively used to frame migrants as disease vectors. Epidemiological complexity is replaced with a simple blame narrative.
publicFear: That outsiders are bringing diseases into the country and authorities are allowing it
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain what the actual epidemiological data shows. Distinguish between disease prevalence, transmission risk, and population-level health patterns. Name what the evidence supports and what it does not.
whatItDoesNotMean: Disease prevalence data is not evidence that migrants cause outbreaks. Public health is a shared infrastructure challenge, not a border-enforcement question.
rapidResponseAdvice: Stick to the epidemiology. Do not dismiss public concern about health infrastructure, but do not allow selective data use to frame people as threats.
humourOptions: Pathogens do not check passports. They also do not read opinion columns.
Blaming disease on outsiders is the oldest public health distortion. It was wrong then too.
exampleNarrative: These diseases were under control until they opened the borders. Now look what's happening.
notes: Historically persistent pattern. Requires careful handling — public health concerns about screening and resources are legitimate; scapegoating is not.

shortDescription: Digital health records, cross-border health data sharing, e-prescriptions, patient portals, and health data governance are reframed as a polite infrastructure for surveillance, profiling, exclusion, or political control.
typicalTopics: AI in healthcare linked to records
likelyDistortion: Digital health infrastructure built for care coordination, research, and interoperability is recast as a deliberate surveillance architecture. Convenience and better outcomes are treated as cover stories for centralised control.
publicFear: That the most intimate data people have — their medical records — is being centralised not for care, but for monitoring, profiling, and eventual coercion
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain what the system actually does, who has access, what governance limits exist, and what the difference is between data sharing for care and data exploitation for control. Name the safeguards before someone else names the fears.
whatItDoesNotMean: Building interoperable health data systems is not the same as building a surveillance state. Access rules, consent frameworks, and governance exist — they may be imperfect, but they are not absent.
rapidResponseAdvice: Do not dismiss privacy concerns as irrational. Acknowledge the legitimate tension between data utility and data protection. Then be specific about what this system does and does not allow.
humourOptions: Your medical file is not a control panel. It is mostly a list of things your GP has been meaning to follow up on.
If governments wanted to track you efficiently, your health records would be the worst possible route. Have you seen how long interoperability takes?
exampleNarrative: What they call digital health is really a system for tracking your body, your choices, and your future.
notes: Distinct from F16 (digital medicine as surveillance) which focuses on clinical tools. F37 targets the governance and infrastructure layer — data spaces, cross-border sharing, and legislative frameworks like EHDS. Particularly active in EU policy discourse.

shortDescription: When a medicine or vaccine becomes available quickly, the speed itself is recast as proof that safety was compromised, side effects were ignored, or harm was knowingly accepted for profit, politics, or institutional prestige.
likelyDistortion: Regulatory speed — designed to respond to urgency, unmet need, or rolling review — is reframed as institutional recklessness. Side effects are not risks to be monitored but hidden costs the system was always willing to impose.
publicFear: That the medicine or vaccine was approved before anyone truly understood what it could do to people, and that regulators chose speed over safety
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain what accelerated or conditional approval actually means, what safety data was required before authorisation, what monitoring continues after launch, and how this differs from skipping safety steps.
whatItDoesNotMean: Faster review does not mean fewer safety requirements. It typically means overlapping processes, rolling data submission, or prioritised review — not reduced evidence thresholds.
rapidResponseAdvice: Do not dismiss the concern as irrational. Explain what was done, what was known at the time of approval, and what monitoring is ongoing. Speed and care are not opposites — say so plainly.
humourOptions: Fast-track approval does not mean someone signed a permission slip on a napkin. It means the queue moved.
If regulators were as careless as this story implies, the paperwork alone would have stopped them.
exampleNarrative: If it reached the public this fast, they clearly did not care what it might do to people.
notes: Hybrid frame: functions as both a fear-based simplifier (speed = danger) and an institutional betrayal story (regulators chose politics or profit over safety). Particularly potent post-pandemic but applies to any accelerated approval pathway including oncology and rare diseases.

shortDescription: Pregnancy is reframed as a condition in which bodily autonomy becomes negotiable and outside authority gains moral standing over medical judgment.
likelyDistortion: Medical complexity in pregnancy is reduced to a moral hierarchy in which preserving pregnancy becomes a higher duty than respecting autonomy, comfort, or sometimes even maternal health. Intervention is suspect, refusal is selfish, and nuance is recast as moral evasion.
publicFear: That acknowledging maternal autonomy means devaluing pregnancy, and that medical decisions during pregnancy are really moral ones in disguise
whatToClarifyUpfront: Explain the specific medical context, who makes the decision, what clinical evidence applies, and why pregnancy does not suspend the right to informed, individual medical judgment.
whatItDoesNotMean: Acknowledging maternal autonomy does not mean dismissing pregnancy. Medical decisions in pregnancy are clinical decisions, not moral verdicts.
rapidResponseAdvice: Do not get drawn into abstract moral debate. Stay with the specific clinical situation, the specific patient population, and the specific medical question. Autonomy and care are not opposites.
humourOptions: Pregnancy is not a jurisdiction. It is a medical condition in which two sets of needs exist at once, and pretending otherwise helps neither.
The body does not stop belonging to the person inside it just because someone else is also inside it.
exampleNarrative: Once there is a pregnancy, the body is no longer just yours to decide over.
notes: Body-purity frame with strong overlap into identity-grievance and control narratives. Particularly activated by legal cases, policy debates, and high-profile maternal health emergencies. Distinct from F33 (fertility panic) which focuses on hormonal/chemical threats to reproduction.

shortDescription: Contraception is reframed not merely as a medical or hormonal issue, but as a civilisational and moral threat: something that severs sex from consequence, weakens women, disrupts fertility, and serves a wider anti-family or anti-life agenda.
likelyDistortion: Contraception is cast as culturally corrosive and morally suspect — undermining proper womanhood, detaching sexuality from responsibility, reducing respect for life, weakening families, and serving a broader ideological project hostile to fertility, motherhood, or social order.
publicFear: That contraception is part of a wider moral decline — damaging femininity, fertility, and social order while disguising itself as empowerment
whatToClarifyUpfront: Distinguish between medical choice and moral judgment. Clarify what contraception actually does, what it does not do, and how individual medical decisions differ from civilisational narratives.
whatItDoesNotMean: Choosing or discussing contraception does not imply participation in moral decline, nor does it indicate weakness, corruption, or ideological capture.
rapidResponseAdvice: Separate the medical reality from the moral narrative. Contraception is a tool with benefits and trade-offs — not a symbol of cultural collapse. Stay with the specific health context.
humourOptions: The pill is a medication, not a manifesto.
Hormones do not have political opinions.
exampleNarrative: What they call reproductive freedom is really chemical alienation dressed up as empowerment.
notes: Body-purity frame that treats contraception as moral contamination. Often overlaps with F33 (fertility panic), F39 (pregnancy jurisdiction), and civilisational decline narratives. Activated by social media 'coming off birth control' content, religious rhetoric, and fertility anxiety discourse.

shortDescription: Advanced, near-universal medical cures are imagined as already existing but withheld from the public — reserved for elites or suppressed to protect existing medical and pharmaceutical systems.
likelyDistortion: Real, effective cures exist but are deliberately kept from the public to maintain pharmaceutical profits or elite privilege.
publicFear: Being denied access to life-saving technology that exists but is intentionally withheld
whatToClarifyUpfront: What stage the research is actually at, what evidence exists, and what barriers to access really look like.
whatItDoesNotMean: This does not prove that effective cures are being hidden or that public healthcare is intentionally limited.
rapidResponseAdvice: Be transparent about research timelines, regulatory requirements, and genuine access barriers without validating conspiracy narratives.
humourOptions: If the elites had a healing pod, someone would have leaked the unboxing video by now.
exampleNarrative: They already have the technology to cure this. You're just not meant to access it.
notes: Distinct from cheap natural cure narratives — this imagines high-tech, sci-fi level medicine as already existing but elite-reserved. Blends technological optimism with institutional distrust.

shortDescription: Illness is reframed not as a medical condition requiring treatment, but as the outward manifestation of unresolved psychological, emotional, spiritual, or moral imbalance.
likelyDistortion: Medical treatment is recast as suppression rather than care. Drugs merely silence the body's 'truth.' Illness becomes something the patient has, at some level, brought on themselves by repressing emotion, living 'wrongly', or failing to resolve trauma.
publicFear: That illness reflects personal failure — that the sick are somehow responsible for their condition through unresolved inner conflict, and that medical treatment is just avoidance
whatToClarifyUpfront: The difference between mind-body connections as one factor among many, and the claim that inner conflict is the sole or primary cause of disease requiring moral or spiritual correction rather than medical care.
whatItDoesNotMean: Acknowledging stress or trauma as health factors does not mean medication is avoidance, or that persistent illness reflects personal failure to resolve deeper issues.
rapidResponseAdvice: Distinguish between holistic care as complement and holistic absolutism as replacement. Acknowledge the desire for meaning without validating the implication that medical treatment suppresses truth or that patients are responsible for their illness.
humourOptions: The body keeps the score. But the scoreboard does not determine the treatment plan.
Trauma-informed care is not the same as trauma-determined diagnosis.
exampleNarrative: The illness is not the real problem. It is your body trying to tell you what your life refuses to face.
notes: Hope-merchant frame that blends legitimate trauma research with moral absolutism. Often overlaps with F33 (fertility panic), F40 (contraception as moral corruption), and natural body absolutism. Can turn illness into a test of virtue and shift blame onto patients.

shortDescription: Collapses every disease into one dietary villain you must eliminate.
likelyDistortion: One molecule is elevated to the master cause of nearly all illness.
publicFear: That a single hidden ingredient in ordinary food is silently making everyone sick.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Disease is multi-factorial; single-substance stories rarely explain outcomes.
whatItDoesNotMean: Noticing that diet matters is not the same as accepting one-cause explanations.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name the appeal of simple stories, then restore the multi-factor picture without dismissing dietary concern.
exampleNarrative: Sugar — or seed oils, or gluten — is what's really making everyone sick.
notes: One-cause-one-cure frame focused on diet.

shortDescription: Sells one diet or regimen as the fix for everything.
likelyDistortion: A single lifestyle regimen is presented as universal cure and moral test.
publicFear: That being sick means you lacked the discipline to follow the right protocol.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Diet matters, but no single regimen cures all chronic disease.
whatItDoesNotMean: Interest in nutrition or lifestyle change is not the same as protocol absolutism.
rapidResponseAdvice: Separate the value of lifestyle change from the moralised promise of universal cure.
exampleNarrative: Go keto, carnivore, or fasting and your body will heal itself.
notes: One-cause-one-cure frame with a virtue/discipline overlay.

shortDescription: Claims you can starve a tumour by cutting sugar or carbs.
likelyDistortion: Real research on tumour metabolism is flattened into 'diet replaces treatment.'
publicFear: That treatment is unnecessary if the diet is strict enough.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Tumour metabolism is studied, but diet is not a substitute for cancer treatment.
whatItDoesNotMean: Discussing nutrition during cancer care is not the same as replacing treatment.
rapidResponseAdvice: Acknowledge the science that exists, then draw the line at treatment substitution.
exampleNarrative: Cancer feeds on sugar, so keto or fasting will starve it — no need for treatment.
notes: One-cause-one-cure frame in the cancer & metabolism terrain.

shortDescription: Treats illness as the just punishment for how someone lived.
likelyDistortion: Statistical risk is converted into moral desert applied to individuals.
publicFear: Onlooker reassurance that illness happens to the careless, not to me.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Risk factors are population-level, not verdicts on individual patients.
whatItDoesNotMean: Talking about prevention is not the same as blaming the sick.
rapidResponseAdvice: Separate risk from blame; name the harm blame does to care.
exampleNarrative: They smoked, ate badly, didn't look after themselves — no wonder they got sick.
notes: Self-blame frame that comforts the healthy at the expense of the sick.

shortDescription: Blames cancer on repressed emotions or unhealed trauma.
likelyDistortion: Wellbeing research is stretched into a psychic aetiology of tumours.
publicFear: That illness proves an inner failing the patient could have prevented.
whatToClarifyUpfront: There is no 'cancer personality,' and trauma does not cause tumours.
whatItDoesNotMean: Caring about stress and wellbeing is not the same as blaming patients for cancer.
rapidResponseAdvice: Honour the value of mental health without conceding a psychic cause for disease.
exampleNarrative: Cancer is your body expressing the feelings you never let yourself feel.
notes: Self-blame frame in the mind & body terrain.

shortDescription: Turns birth-rate data into a verdict on women's choices. Economics, housing and men's role vanish from the equation.
likelyDistortion: Falling birth rates are the bill for women's ambition, and the fix is women stepping back.
publicFear: That the future is being cancelled by a generation of women who chose themselves.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Fertility tracks housing costs, childcare, job security and partnership patterns for both sexes. Countries with the highest female employment are not the ones with the lowest birth rates.
whatItDoesNotMean: Discussing demography is not blaming women. The distortion arrives when one variable is chosen as the culprit and the rest are erased.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name the other variables on the first line: housing, childcare, men's hours, insecurity. Refuse the single-culprit framing before arguing the numbers.
humourOptions: If careers caused childlessness, the 1950s would have been a fertility desert for every man in a suit.
exampleNarrative: Women were told to chase careers, and now there are no children.
notes: Feeds the men–women and tradition–progress fault lines; pairs with F55 on the opposite pole.

shortDescription: Turns research on changing family and labour patterns into proof that men have been written off. Every statistic becomes an insult.
likelyDistortion: Modern society has quietly decided men are surplus, so every change is an attack.
publicFear: That belonging and purpose have been withdrawn from half the population without a vote.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Changes in family and labour patterns are shifts in roles, not verdicts on a sex. Most of the data show men and women both adapting, unevenly and under stress.
whatItDoesNotMean: Real hardship among men — education, suicide, loneliness — is not a manosphere talking point. The distortion is turning hardship into rejection by design.
rapidResponseAdvice: Acknowledge the specific hardship before contesting the story. A man who feels written off will not hear statistics until he hears that.
humourOptions: Society has not decided it no longer needs men. It has decided it no longer needs a specific 1955 model, and the recall notice went out slowly.
exampleNarrative: Society has decided it no longer needs men.
notes: Pairs with F56 on the opposite pole; the two frames screenshot each other.

frameName: The pill picks the wrong men
shortDescription: Inflates small, contested mate-preference studies into a master explanation of relationship breakdown, with women's biology as the hidden culprit.
triggerWords: the pill changes who you love
come off the pill and see
likelyDistortion: Women's biology, altered by the pill, is the hidden reason relationships fail.
publicFear: That an intimate choice has been silently rewiring the most important decisions of a life.
whatToClarifyUpfront: A few small studies suggested hormonal contraception might shift mate preferences; larger replication attempts largely failed to confirm it. Relationship breakdown has many well-documented causes; this is not among the established ones.
whatItDoesNotMean: Asking about side effects of contraception is legitimate. The distortion is a small, unreplicated finding promoted to a master explanation.
rapidResponseAdvice: State the replication record in one sentence. Then move to what is actually known about contraception's effects.
humourOptions: If the pill really chose partners, pharmacists would run the best dating agencies in the country.
exampleNarrative: Hormonal contraception changes who women fall for — that is why marriages fail.
notes: Male twin of F40; borrows purity logic (FL2) as well as the gender wedge (FL6).

shortDescription: Turns endocrinological trend data into a story of civilisational softening, then sells the fix. The male twin of F33.
likelyDistortion: Men are biologically weakening, and modern life — or modern women — did it.
publicFear: That masculinity itself is being chemically eroded.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Population-level testosterone declines have been reported and are studied; the likely drivers are obesity, sedentary life, sleep and age structure. None of this is evidence of civilisational decline, and none of it is fixed by a supplement.
whatItDoesNotMean: Endocrine trends are real research questions. The distortion is the leap from a lab value to a verdict on a civilisation, usually with a checkout page attached.
rapidResponseAdvice: Separate the measurement from the story and name who profits from the story.
humourOptions: Testosterone has been declining for decades. So has the price of a TRT consultation, which is the part of the trend nobody advertises.
exampleNarrative: Testosterone has fallen one percent a year. No wonder men are weak.
notes: Male twin of F33; sells the fix (cui bono: supplement and TRT sellers).

shortDescription: Turns a domestic social movement into an enemy programme. Any gender-related finding becomes evidence of the import.
likelyDistortion: Feminism is not a domestic movement but a foreign programme to dismantle families and nations.
publicFear: That the most intimate arrangements of life are being rewritten from outside.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Women's movements in every European country have domestic histories older than any of today's foreign actors. Treating a social movement as an import ends the argument before it starts.
whatItDoesNotMean: Criticising specific feminist positions is normal politics. The distortion is attributing a whole movement to an enemy.
rapidResponseAdvice: Refuse the import frame; return to the specific policy and its domestic history.
humourOptions: If feminism were a foreign operation, it would be the only one in history that started with local women demanding the vote in their own language.
exampleNarrative: Feminism was imported to break our families.
notes: Documented pro-Kremlin narrative (EUvsDisinfo; SAGE 2026). Pairs with F54.

frameName: Criticism of feminism as foreign operation
shortDescription: The mirror of F53. Turns any critique — including reasonable ones — into evidence of hostile influence, which closes the debate and feeds the other pole.
likelyDistortion: Any criticism of feminism is hostile influence, so it need not be answered.
publicFear: That the ground is already contaminated and no critic can be sincere.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Hostile actors do amplify anti-feminist content — and also benefit when every critic is labelled an agent, because that closes debate and feeds the other pole. Answer the argument; document the amplification separately.
whatItDoesNotMean: Noting real coordinated amplification is not this frame. The distortion is using attribution as a substitute for argument.
rapidResponseAdvice: Answer the substance in one line, then — if there is evidence — describe the amplification as a separate fact.
humourOptions: Not everyone who disagrees with you is on a payroll. Some people do it for free, which is arguably worse.
exampleNarrative: Anyone questioning feminism is reading from a Kremlin script.
notes: Mirror of F53. State-actor evidence for this pole is weaker; included because the wedge needs both poles.

shortDescription: Dismisses real data on men's outcomes as a political manoeuvre. The dismissal is then screenshotted by the other pole as proof of F50.
likelyDistortion: Men's problems are a political manoeuvre, so the data can be dismissed.
publicFear: That attention given to men will be taken from women.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Male suicide rates, boys' educational outcomes and loneliness measures are real and well documented. Dismissing them does not weaken the other pole — it is its best recruitment material.
whatItDoesNotMean: Pointing out that the manosphere exploits these issues is accurate. The distortion is denying the issues to deny the exploiters.
rapidResponseAdvice: Grant the data first. Then contest what is built on them.
humourOptions: The male crisis is real. The people selling a cure in a four-hour podcast are the other crisis.
exampleNarrative: Male suicide, school failure, loneliness — reactionary talking points.
notes: Pairs with F49; its dismissals are screenshotted as proof of F50.

shortDescription: Turns crime statistics into a categorical verdict on half the population. Comforting as a rule of thumb, corrosive as a public claim, and gold for F50.
likelyDistortion: Statistics justify treating every man as a threat.
publicFear: That safety requires suspicion of half the population.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Most violence is committed by a small minority of men; base rates do not license categorical verdicts. The frame comforts as a rule of thumb and corrodes as a public claim.
whatItDoesNotMean: Women's safety concerns are legitimate and grounded. The distortion is converting a base rate into a category.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name the base rate and the minority. Do not argue about the bear.
humourOptions: Man or bear is a fine thought experiment. It is a poor demographic policy.
exampleNarrative: The safest assumption is that any man is a danger.
notes: Pairs with F50. Evidence of organised amplification on this pole is thin; included on mechanism and case grounds.

frameName: The system is rigged for women
shortDescription: Turns selective statistics on custody, education or hiring into a picture of a state that has switched sides. Every policy becomes evidence.
likelyDistortion: Every institution has switched sides against men.
publicFear: That the state has become an adversary in the most personal matters.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Family courts, schools and hiring show mixed and context-specific patterns; some disadvantage men, some women. A rigged-system story needs all of them to point one way, and they do not.
whatItDoesNotMean: Specific inequities affecting men deserve attention. The distortion is the totalising 'system' claim.
rapidResponseAdvice: Pick the specific inequity, agree where true, and refuse the totalising claim.
humourOptions: If the system were rigged for women, boardrooms would look different and so would the pay slips.
exampleNarrative: Courts, schools, hiring — the whole system runs against men.
notes: Manosphere staple (UN Women 2025). Pairs with F55.

shortDescription: Sells a single social protocol for every modern ailment. The gender twin of F45. Frequently packaged with Russia as the place where it already works.
likelyDistortion: Loneliness, anxiety and falling births are all cured by restoring traditional roles.
publicFear: That modern life has broken something simple that used to work.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Countries that promote traditional roles most loudly do not have the best outcomes on any of these measures; Russia has one of the world's highest divorce rates. One social protocol does not treat five different problems.
whatItDoesNotMean: Valuing family life is not this frame. The distortion is one prescription for everything, with a foreign showroom attached.
rapidResponseAdvice: Ask which of the five problems it fixes, and cite the showroom's own numbers.
humourOptions: The traditional order is available for inspection in countries that advertise it. Bring a divorce statistician.
exampleNarrative: Go back to the natural order and the loneliness, the anxiety and the birth rate fix themselves.
notes: Gender twin of F45. EUvsDisinfo documents the 'Russia as women's paradise' showroom. Pairs with F59.

shortDescription: Turns a grievance into a total programme of withdrawal and sells it as freedom. The mirror of F58: one social protocol, opposite direction.
likelyDistortion: The only rational response to men is total withdrawal, and this is freedom.
publicFear: That engagement with men is a losing game by design.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Grievances behind the withdrawal are often real. A total programme sold as liberation is still one social protocol for everything, and it hands the other pole its proof.
whatItDoesNotMean: Choosing to be single is not this frame. The distortion is prescribing withdrawal as the only rational option.
rapidResponseAdvice: Honour the grievance, refuse the totality, and note who screenshots it.
humourOptions: Withdrawal as a movement has one structural weakness: it needs the other side to keep showing up to be withdrawn from.
exampleNarrative: The only rational response is to stop dating men altogether.
notes: Mirror of F58.

shortDescription: Turns findings on sex differences into an ideological act. The mirror of F21: there, social science is ideology; here, biology is. Both close the paper before reading it.
likelyDistortion: Any finding of a sex difference is ideology and can be dismissed unread.
publicFear: That biology will be used to justify inequality.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Some sex-difference research is weak and some is strong; the field has real methodological debates. Dismissing all of it as patriarchy closes the paper as surely as F21 closes the social sciences.
whatItDoesNotMean: Criticising bad methods is science. The distortion is treating the topic itself as disqualifying.
rapidResponseAdvice: Separate the method critique from the topic ban; welcome the first, refuse the second.
humourOptions: Some evolutionary psychology is a just-so story. So is some of the criticism, and neither gets a pass for tone.
exampleNarrative: Any study that finds a sex difference is patriarchy with a p-value.
notes: Mirror of F21. Included for symmetry; no state-actor evidence.

shortDescription: Recasts a woman's argument as an emotional state. Nothing needs to be refuted, because nothing was said.
likelyDistortion: A woman's argument is a mood and therefore needs no reply.
publicFear: Not a public fear — a control move: the audience is invited to stop listening.
whatToClarifyUpfront: An argument is judged on its content. Recasting it as an emotional state is a way of not answering it — and is applied to women at a rate men rarely experience.
whatItDoesNotMean: Noting that a statement was angry is not the frame. The distortion is substituting the mood for the content.
rapidResponseAdvice: Do not defend your tone. Restate the claim in one line and ask for the counter-argument.
humourOptions: If having feelings disqualified people from analysis, the comment section would be silent.
exampleNarrative: She is not analysing. She is having feelings.
notes: Attack on the messenger, not the claim. EU DisinfoLab; ELNET 2026.

shortDescription: Replaces the claim with the payroll. Iakimova's Bulgarian epithets — sorosoid, grantoed — are the industrial version.
likelyDistortion: The speaker is on someone's payroll, so the claim is void.
publicFear: That nobody in public speaks for free, so nobody speaks honestly.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Funding is disclosed and can be examined; it does not decide the truth of a claim. 'Grant-fed', 'Soros-paid' and their local variants are propaganda epithets, not evidence.
whatItDoesNotMean: Asking for conflict-of-interest disclosure is proper. The distortion is treating any funding as guilt.
rapidResponseAdvice: Disclose in one line, then return to the claim. Never chase the epithet.
humourOptions: Yes, someone pays me. It is called a salary and it is disappointingly public.
exampleNarrative: Follow the money. Who pays her?
notes: Iakimova et al. 2025 document the industrialised version ('sorosoid', 'grantoed').

shortDescription: Makes reproductive status a credential. Works on paediatricians, educators, demographers and politicians alike.
triggerWords: what does she know about kids
likelyDistortion: Only a parent may speak about children, families or fertility.
publicFear: That decisions about families are made by people who have none.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Expertise on children's health or demography comes from training and evidence, not from reproductive status. The frame is applied almost exclusively to women.
whatItDoesNotMean: Lived experience is valuable. The distortion is making it a licence and revoking the licence from one sex.
rapidResponseAdvice: Do not disclose or defend your family life. Name the qualification that matters and continue.
humourOptions: Oncologists are not required to have cancer. The rule is oddly specific to children and women.
exampleNarrative: What does a childless woman know about children's health?
notes: ELNET 2026 documents attacks via motherhood.

shortDescription: Replies to the body instead of the claim. Women scientists receive appearance comments at roughly ten times the rate of men.
likelyDistortion: How she looks is a fair reply to what she said.
publicFear: Not a public fear — a pricing move: visibility is made costly.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Comments on appearance are a reply to nothing. In a Spanish survey of scientists (N=237) women reported them at roughly ten times the rate of men.
whatItDoesNotMean: Nothing legitimate lives here.
rapidResponseAdvice: Ignore entirely. Any reply confirms the price.
humourOptions: Peer review has many flaws, but it has never once asked what the author was wearing.
exampleNarrative: Climate Barbie.
notes: EU DisinfoLab (McKenna case); JCOM 2026.

shortDescription: Turns visibility itself into the motive. The more the claim travels, the more the frame confirms itself.
triggerWords: she just wants to be seen
likelyDistortion: Visibility is the motive, so the content is performance.
publicFear: That public voices are performing rather than informing.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Public communication is part of the job of experts and public figures. The frame makes reach itself the evidence against the speaker, so it can never be answered by reaching fewer people.
whatItDoesNotMean: Some public communication is performative. The distortion is making motive a substitute for content.
rapidResponseAdvice: Do not explain why you are visible. Answer the content or say nothing.
humourOptions: Communicating in public in order to be heard is, admittedly, a suspicious strategy for communication.
exampleNarrative: She only says it to be seen.
notes: ELNET 2026; case material 2026.

shortDescription: Attacks the credential rather than the content. Women are challenged on competence a third more often than men in the same role.
triggerWords: where did she get that degree
likelyDistortion: The credential is doubtful, so the claim is.
publicFear: That authority is claimed rather than earned.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Credentials are checkable and usually checked. The frame is applied to women a third more often than to men in the same roles, which tells you what it is measuring.
whatItDoesNotMean: Checking credentials is legitimate. The distortion is asking the question of one sex as a reflex.
rapidResponseAdvice: State the credential once, plainly. Do not re-litigate it.
humourOptions: The degree is on the wall. The wall is on the internet. The internet has not read it.
exampleNarrative: Where did she even get that degree?
notes: JCOM 2026 (Spain, N=237): competence challenged 34.3% of women vs 24.2% of men.

shortDescription: Pulls partners, children and past into the argument. The aim is not to win but to make holding the position too expensive.
likelyDistortion: Her partner, family or past decide the claim — and the cost of continuing.
publicFear: Not a public fear — a pricing move against the speaker's people.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Private life is not an argument. The aim of the frame is not to win but to make holding a public position too expensive to keep; it works by pulling in people who never entered the debate.
whatItDoesNotMean: Genuine conflicts of interest involving relatives are disclosable. The distortion is biography as evidence and family as leverage.
rapidResponseAdvice: Document, report, do not engage. Route through the institution, not the personal account.
exampleNarrative: Look who she is married to.
notes: ELNET 2026: partners and children drawn in; OSCE/ODIHR toolkit.

shortDescription: Recasts internal criticism as betrayal of the group. The frame is symmetrical: it is used by every pole against its own dissenters.
likelyDistortion: Criticism from inside the group is betrayal of the group.
publicFear: That dissent from inside weakens the group at the moment it is under attack.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Internal criticism is how groups correct themselves. The frame is symmetrical: every pole uses it against its own dissenters, and it works because belonging feels like survival.
whatItDoesNotMean: Groups may disagree with a member. The distortion is treating disagreement as defection.
rapidResponseAdvice: Refuse the loyalty test explicitly; restate the criticism as care for the group's credibility.
humourOptions: Being called a traitor by both sides on the same afternoon is, in this field, a form of peer review.
exampleNarrative: A woman attacking women. A scientist attacking science.
notes: Taboo layer 'identity and group discipline' made explicit; case material 2026.

shortDescription: Turns an incident into a false flag. Whoever warned about it becomes the suspect.
likelyDistortion: The incident was staged by the people who warned about it.
publicFear: That governments manufacture threats to manage their populations.
whatToClarifyUpfront: False-flag claims arrive within hours, before any investigation, and never require evidence. Ask what would count as proof and note that the claim was made before it could exist.
whatItDoesNotMean: Asking for attribution evidence is proper. The distortion is attribution to the warner by default.
rapidResponseAdvice: Say what is known, what is not, and when more will be known. Do not argue the plot.
humourOptions: The false-flag theory arrives before the investigators, which is impressive logistics for a cover-up.
exampleNarrative: The drone was a provocation approved in Brussels.
notes: EDMO 2025 drone incidents; Iakimova on 'confirmation through denial'.

shortDescription: Turns a threat assessment into a sales pitch. Works identically for defence, pharma and public health.
likelyDistortion: Every warning is an invoice.
publicFear: That we are being frightened for someone's profit.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Warnings and procurement can both be examined separately. The frame merges them so that any threat assessment becomes self-serving by definition — and works identically for defence, pharma and public health.
whatItDoesNotMean: Scrutinising spending is democracy. The distortion is treating the warning as evidence of the sale.
rapidResponseAdvice: Show the warning's source and the budget's process as two separate things with two separate dates.
humourOptions: If warnings were invoices, meteorologists would be the richest people in the country.
exampleNarrative: Every warning is an invoice for the arms industry.
notes: EDMO 2025 (arms-industry conspiracy after drone crashes).

shortDescription: Turns any defensive measure into the first step to catastrophe. The only safe option becomes doing nothing.
likelyDistortion: Any defensive measure is the first step to catastrophe, so doing nothing is the only safe option.
publicFear: That defence itself is what will get us killed.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Escalation is a real strategic question with real analysts. The frame replaces the question with a reflex, so that every response is a countdown and inaction is dressed as peace.
whatItDoesNotMean: Debating proportionality is proper. The distortion is that only one direction of error is ever counted.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name both risks — acting and not acting — and who bears each.
humourOptions: The escalation frame has predicted forty of the last zero nuclear wars.
exampleNarrative: Say the word and we are in a nuclear war.
notes: EDMO 2025 (uncontrolled escalation narrative across platforms).

shortDescription: Turns an outbreak or attack into a pretext designed in advance. The plandemic template, portable to any threat.
likelyDistortion: The emergency was designed in advance for control.
publicFear: That emergencies are a technique of government.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Outbreaks and attacks have investigable origins; the plandemic template needs none and fits every threat. Its tell is that it arrives complete, with the cure and the villain already attached.
whatItDoesNotMean: Investigating origins is science. The distortion is a template that answers before the question.
rapidResponseAdvice: Give the honest uncertainty on origin and the concrete measures, dated. Do not fight the template head-on.
humourOptions: A plan that requires every health ministry on earth to keep a secret is the least plausible part of the story.
exampleNarrative: They engineer the threat so they can lock us down.
notes: EDMO 2026 hantavirus (plandemic, lab origin, secret vaccines, miracle cures, electoral angle).

frameName: The threat is a pretext against us
shortDescription: Turns counter-measures into persecution of ordinary people. Regulation of manipulation becomes proof of manipulation.
triggerWords: hybrid threat is just a word
likelyDistortion: Counter-measures against manipulation are persecution of ordinary people.
publicFear: That the fight against manipulation is a fight against us.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Regulating coordinated manipulation and silencing citizens are different things and can be told apart by what they target. The frame needs them confused.
whatItDoesNotMean: Debating the limits of regulation is legitimate. The distortion is that any defence is repression.
rapidResponseAdvice: Say exactly what is targeted (behaviour, coordination, inauthenticity) and what is not (opinion).
humourOptions: The people loudest about being silenced are, as a rule, extremely audible.
exampleNarrative: 'Hybrid threat' is just the new word for censoring patriots.
notes: Iakimova et al. 2025 (regulation framed as censorship); sibling of F07.

shortDescription: Turns a warning about external actors into a hunt for internal ones. Migrants, minorities and critics become the threat that was announced.
likelyDistortion: The warning about an external actor is really about the enemy next door.
publicFear: That the danger has already come inside.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Hybrid threats are conducted by specific actors and can be described specifically. The frame swaps the actor for a domestic category — migrants, minorities, critics — and turns a warning into a hunt.
whatItDoesNotMean: Counter-intelligence is specific by nature. The distortion is replacing specificity with a group.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name the actual actor and method. Refuse the substitution explicitly.
humourOptions: If the fifth column were as large as advertised, it would need its own parking.
exampleNarrative: The real threat is the fifth column in our own streets.
notes: SAGE 2026 narrative 5 (migrant threat, fabricated statistics); sibling of F35.

shortDescription: Turns cohort economics into a theft. Structural causes become a generation's character.
likelyDistortion: One generation took what another was owed.
publicFear: That the future has already been spent by someone else.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Cohort differences in housing, pensions and climate exposure are real and structural. Structure has causes; a generation is not one of them. The frame turns policy into character.
whatItDoesNotMean: Intergenerational fairness is a real policy question. The distortion is answering it with a culprit.
rapidResponseAdvice: Name the policy lever, not the cohort.
humourOptions: Boomers did not steal the houses. They bought them at prices that now look like a typo.
exampleNarrative: Boomers took the houses, the pensions and the climate.
notes: Protect Democracy 2025 finds the youth deficit structural, not generational — the frame erases exactly that.

shortDescription: Turns mental-health data into a verdict on character. Rising diagnosis becomes falling resilience.
likelyDistortion: Rising diagnoses prove a generation cannot cope.
publicFear: That the next generation will not be able to run things.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Diagnosis rates rise with awareness, access and changed criteria as well as with prevalence; the research disagreement is real. Character is not one of the variables.
whatItDoesNotMean: Asking what drives the numbers is science. The distortion is a verdict on temperament.
rapidResponseAdvice: Separate prevalence from reporting in one sentence, then stop.
humourOptions: Every generation has been called soft by the one that made the world it grew up in.
exampleNarrative: They cannot handle a hard word. Snowflakes.
notes: Pairs with F74.

frameName: The old are voting us into the grave
shortDescription: Turns demographic voting patterns into an argument against the franchise. Solidarity between generations becomes zero-sum.
likelyDistortion: Older voters decide a future they will not live in, so their votes count less.
publicFear: That the ballot is rigged by demography.
whatToClarifyUpfront: Age differences in turnout and preferences are real; they are arguments for participation, not against the franchise. The frame turns a demographic fact into a solidarity-ending one.
whatItDoesNotMean: Discussing representation gaps is legitimate. The distortion is the step from gap to disenfranchisement.
rapidResponseAdvice: Show the participation gap and the remedy (turnout, candidacy), not the culprit.
humourOptions: Democracy has always been decided by the people who show up. The remedy has never been fewer of them.
exampleNarrative: People who will not live with the consequences decide everything.
notes: Protect Democracy 2025: Congress median age 65/58; the report attributes the gap to structure.
